Hi, I'm Pieter, and I live in Utrecht, in the Netherlands. People say the Dutch are very direct, and well, it's true. We are not great at small talk. At a party, I might ask you how much you paid for your house, or why you don't have children. For us, these questions are harmless. I mean, we are just curious. The first time I visited a friend in Texas, a woman at the supermarket asked me, how are you doing? So I told her. My back hurt, my flight was late, and I missed my wife. She just smiled and walked away. Actually, she did not want an answer at all. It was just hello. By the way, the weather is the one topic that is safe everywhere, even in Holland, because it is always bad. Anyway, now when an American asks me how I am, I say, good, thanks, and you? Ten seconds. Done.

Hello, I'm Priya. I grew up in Chennai, in the south of India, and now I live in London. In India, small talk is very personal. An auntie you meet at a wedding will ask, are you married? Why not? How much does your husband earn? It is not rude. It is a way of saying, I care about you. In London, I learned that those questions are off-limits. You do not ask about money, age or religion. So what do the British talk about? Well, the weather, the trains, and the weather again. At first, I thought it was boring. I mean, who cares if it is raining? But then I understood. The weather is common ground. Everybody has an opinion, and nobody gets hurt. Actually, now I am the one who starts. When there is a lull in the conversation, I say, lovely day, isn't it? Even when it isn't.
